question: How does a database index make a query faster, and when would it make things slower?
expected_answer: An index is a B-tree (usually) that lets the engine find rows without scanning the table. It speeds up equality and range filters, joins and ORDER BY, at the cost of extra storage and slower writes. It can be slower when selectivity is low, when the query returns most rows, or when the index does not cover the selected columns; unused indexes still cost on every insert, update and delete.
answer: A B-tree index keeps keys sorted so the planner can seek instead of scanning: it turns an O(n) table scan into roughly O(log n) for equality and range predicates. It also helps joins and ordered reads. It makes things slower when selectivity is low, when the query returns most of the table, or when the index does not cover the projected columns and you pay a lookup per row. Every insert, update and delete also has to maintain the index, so unused indexes are pure overhead.

question: What does @Transactional do in Spring, and when does it silently not work?
expected_answer: It opens a transaction around the annotated method using a proxy: commit on normal return, rollback on RuntimeException. It silently does not apply to self-invocation inside the same bean, to private or final methods, when the class is not a Spring bean, or when the exception is checked and rollbackFor is not set.
answer: Spring wraps the bean in a proxy and starts a transaction before the method, committing on normal return and rolling back on unchecked exceptions. The common traps are self-invocation inside the same bean, private or final methods, and beans you instantiate yourself with new: in all three the proxy is bypassed. Checked exceptions also do not roll back unless rollbackFor is set.

question: How would you make a POST endpoint idempotent for retries?
expected_answer: Accept a client-generated idempotency key, store it with the response under a unique constraint, and return the stored response for a repeated key. Reserve the key before doing the work so concurrent duplicates cannot both execute; make the write itself atomic.
answer: The client sends an Idempotency-Key header. On the first request I insert the key into a unique table together with a status, do the work in the same transaction, and store the response. A retry hits the unique constraint and returns the stored response instead of charging twice. Concurrent duplicates are handled because the insert reserves the key before any side effect, and I return 409 while the first request is still in flight.

question: Design a rate limiter for 100k requests per second across several regions.
expected_answer: Discuss the algorithm (token bucket / sliding window), where state lives (local + Redis with Lua for atomicity), consistency trade-offs, failure mode (fail open vs closed), keying (user/IP/route), clock issues, and observability.
answer: I would use a token bucket per key. Each region keeps a local bucket for the hot path and syncs to Redis with an atomic Lua script every N tokens, so a single global point is not hit per request. The key is tenant plus route, with separate limits for expensive endpoints. If Redis is unavailable we fail open with a conservative local limit and alert, because blocking all traffic is worse than a temporary overshoot. Clock skew is avoided by using Redis time for refills, and I would export allow/deny counters and bucket saturation per region.
